case_studies.title: YAVIN: A Unified Architecture for Secure Edge Processing in Memory
case_studies.abstract: Secure, private multi-tenant execution spanning processors, memory, and accelerators remains one of the most significant challenges in modern edge computing systems. Simultaneously, processing-in-memory (PIM) has emerged as an effective approach for reducing the Von Neumann bottleneck by moving computation closer to data. Existing trusted execution environments (TEEs) establish trust only within the processor, protecting data while it traverses untrusted resources such as the memory bus. Consequently, trusted computation cannot be performed directly within memory. We present YAVIN, a unified t
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of secure multi-tenant execution in edge computing by building a unified architecture called YAVIN, which enables trusted computation directly within memory, resulting in improved security and performance. YAVIN combines processing-in-memory and trusted execution environments to address the limitations of existing solutions. This research aims to reduce the Von Neumann bottleneck and improve edge computing security.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage edge computing infrastructure, here is what to do: review your current architecture for potential security vulnerabilities in memory and processor interactions, assess the feasibility of implementing YAVIN or similar architectures, and evaluate the potential performance benefits of processing-in-memory for your specific use case.
case_studies.score_reasoning: This paper presents a novel architecture for secure edge processing that addresses a specific challenge in modern computing systems. It's directly relevant to IT infrastructures and could be used to improve security in various edge computing scenarios, including endpoint management and cloud infrastructure. An IT engineer or consultant could potentially use this architecture to propose a new service to a client and build it within 90 days.

case_studies.title: GUIDE: Governed Unified Intelligence for Document-to-Artifact Generation in Enterprise Settings
case_studies.abstract: Enterprise guideline documents are heterogeneous and multimodal, combining narrative text, complex tables, and embedded images. Existing LLM and VLM systems face hallucinated content, table structure degradation, and lack governed workflows extending beyond extraction to validation and artifact generation. This leaves enterprises to perform this manually, consuming 2-3 days per document. To address this, we introduce GUIDE, a governed multi-agent framework built on a shared versioned rule store with schema-validated inter-agent contracts and end-to-end provenance tracking. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of manually processing complex enterprise guideline documents by building a governed multi-agent framework called GUIDE. GUIDE automates the process of extracting, validating, and generating artifacts from these documents, reducing manual processing time from 2-3 days to potentially near real-time. The result is a more efficient and accurate document-to-artifact generation process.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage document-heavy workflows, here is what to do: review your current document processing systems, identify areas where automation can improve efficiency, and consider implementing a framework like GUIDE to reduce manual processing time. This flags a risk: if your organization relies on manual document processing, check for potential inefficiencies and errors immediately. Not directly applicable to general IT infrastructure work, but relevant to IT consultants working with document-intensive enterprises.
case_studies.score_reasoning: This paper introduces a governed multi-agent framework GUIDE, relevant to IT engineers who manage enterprise document generation. It has implications for MLOps, DevOps automation, and security in terms of data validation and artifact generation. The framework's value can be utilized within 90 days to automate tasks, reduce manual labor, and propose improved services to clients.

case_studies.title: PIPES: Securing Agent Perception with Provenance and Priors
case_studies.abstract: Tool-using agents consume external data from sources with different levels of trust, yet tool responses rarely identify who produced each component or what it should convey. We show that this gap enables state-corruption attacks, in which attacker-controlled content makes environmental claims beyond the informational authority of its response component and corrupts the agent's perceived environment, making the resulting action appear justified to existing guardrails. We introduce PIPES (Provenance-Informed, Prior-Enforced Screening), which screens response units using semantic priors and sourc
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of securing agent perception by identifying trustworthy data sources, the authors built PIPES, a system that screens response units using semantic priors and source provenance, resulting in improved security against state-corruption attacks. PIPES helps prevent attacks that manipulate an agent's perceived environment. It secures tool-using agents that consume external data from various sources.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage AI or machine learning systems that use external data sources, here is what to do: review your current data validation processes, assess the trustworthiness of each data source, and consider implementing a provenance-informed screening system like PIPES to prevent state-corruption attacks. This flags a risk: if your organisation uses tool-using agents, check your current guardrails for potential vulnerabilities. Not directly applicable to general IT infrastructure work, but relevant to AI and machine learning security.

case_studies.title: ERSkill: Evolving for Skill-Guided Adaptive Memory Retrieval
case_studies.abstract: While Large Language Model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on long-term memory for persistent interactions, the retrieval mechanisms governing this memory are rarely treated as evolvable components. This static approach limits performance on heterogeneous memory queries, which often demand diverse evidence construction strategies. To address this, we introduce \textbf{ERSkill}, a retrieval-centric framework for self-evolving, skill-guided memory access. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of limited performance in Large Language Model agents' long-term memory retrieval, introducing ERSkill, a framework for self-evolving memory access, resulting in improved memory query performance. ERSkill compiles interaction histories into a structured memory store and represents retrieval behaviors as executable skills. This research focuses on language model development and is not directly relevant to cloud infrastructure management.

case_studies.title: CAPRI: Contract-Aware Proof Repair for Isabelle
case_studies.abstract: We address the use of large language models (LLMs) to help discover Isabelle proofs. An Isabelle build establishes that the submitted theory is accepted, but not that an LLM changed only what the developer authorised. We present CAPRI, a contract-aware repair workflow in which Isabelle checks the proof and an independent checker enforces a machine-readable edit contract. Prompts, proposals, candidate repositories, diagnostics, verdicts, and hashes are retained for audit. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of ensuring that large language models make authorized changes to Isabelle proofs. The researchers built CAPRI, a contract-aware repair workflow that checks and enforces machine-readable edit contracts. The result is a more secure and transparent proof repair process.

case_studies.title: OpScale: Operator-level Provisioning and Autoscaling for LLM Serving
case_studies.abstract: Achieving cost efficiency while meeting strict user-facing SLOs (e.g., time-to-first-token) remains a fundamental challenge for cloud GPU clusters serving large language models (LLMs). Autoscaling is the key mechanism for cluster resource management, yet a basic system design question is open for serving LLMs: what should be the unit of scaling? Existing approaches primarily treat the entire model as a monolithic scaling unit--simple but unable to capture the fine-grained dynamics of inference workloads. As a result, such coarse-grained scaling often leads to either SLO violations under bursty
case_studies.summary: Researchers built OpScale, a system for provisioning and autoscaling large language models in cloud GPU clusters, to improve cost efficiency while meeting strict user-facing service level objectives. OpScale achieves this by using a finer-grained unit of scaling, rather than treating the entire model as one unit. This results in better resource management and reduced SLO violations.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud GPU clusters for large language models, here is what to do: assess your current autoscaling approach, consider implementing a finer-grained scaling unit like OpScale, and evaluate its impact on cost efficiency and SLO compliance. This flags a risk: if your org uses coarse-grained scaling for LLMs, check for potential SLO violations under bursty workloads immediately. Review your cluster resource management to see if OpScale's approach can be applied to your existing infrastructure.
case_studies.score_reasoning: Paper presents an innovative approach to LLM serving, focusing on operator-level provisioning and autoscaling. This is novel and relevant to IT engineers using cloud GPU clusters.

case_studies.title: On the Structural Limits of Machine Learning Decision Systems: An Information-Theoretic, Interaction-Based, and Stochastic-Dynamical Perspective
case_studies.abstract: Machine learning procedures are commonly evaluated in terms of predictive accuracy and computational efficiency. However, their achievable performance is fundamentally constrained by structural properties of the underlying data-generating process, which are formalized in terms of informational bounds. In this work we examine intrinsic limits of data-driven decision systems from an information-theoretic and interaction-based perspective. We analyze minimal achievable error in classification through Fano-type bounds and precision limits in parametric estimation via the Cramér-Rao inequality, emp
case_studies.summary: This research explores the fundamental limits of machine learning decision systems, examining the structural properties of data that constrain their performance. The authors built a framework to analyze these limits from an information-theoretic and interaction-based perspective. The result highlights the intrinsic bounds on achievable performance in machine learning, which may impact the design of certain AI systems.

case_studies.title: Does Fixing Break Security? An Empirical Study of Security Degradation in Iterative LLM-Driven Infrastructure-as-Code Repair
case_studies.abstract: Background: Iterative feedback loops are the dominant paradigm for improving LLM-generated Infrastructure-as-Code (IaC): validators such as Checkov and terraform validate feed error signals back for successive repair attempts. Prior work reports cumulative-best metrics, which are non-decreasing by construction, so the raw per-iteration security trajectory has never been examined for IaC. case_studies.summary: This research investigates if using machine learning models to automatically fix issues in cloud infrastructure code can accidentally introduce new security problems. The researchers built a system to test and measure the security impact of these automatic fixes. The result shows that security can degrade during the repair process.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure that uses automated code repair tools, here is what to do: step 1, review your current security settings, step 2, test the automated fixes for potential security regressions, step 3, consider implementing additional security checks to catch any introduced vulnerabilities.

However, it does address a security concern specific to IT infrastructure management and deployment. A potential IT consultant might be interested in using this study to inform their own security assessments or to advise clients on mitigating security regression.
